cards.front: What legislation established the Federal Reserve System, and what is its primary purpose?
cards.back: The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 established the Fed as the central bank of the United States to provide a safer, more flexible, and more stable monetary and financial system.

cards.front: What are the two primary duties of the Federal Reserve Board (FRB)?
cards.back: (1) Conduct the nation's monetary policy to promote maximum employment, and (2) promote a stable price environment by keeping inflation under control.

cards.front: Monetary policy
cards.back: The Federal Reserve's management of the money supply—the amount of cash available within the U.S. economy—to influence employment, prices, and economic growth.

cards.front: Who is considered the founder of monetarist theory, on which much of the Fed's work is based?
cards.back: Milton Friedman, PhD.

cards.front: M1 (money supply)
cards.back: The most readily available money to spend: cash (currency and coin) and demand deposit accounts such as checking accounts.

cards.front: M2 (money supply)
cards.back: M1 plus consumer savings deposits — savings accounts, retail (nonnegotiable) CDs, money market funds, and overnight repurchase agreements (repos).

cards.front: M3 (money supply)
cards.back: M2 plus large time deposits, such as negotiable (jumbo) CDs and multiday repurchase agreements (repos).

cards.front: Seabird Airlines has funds in a long-term jumbo CD. When the CD matures, Seabird moves the proceeds into a checking account. What is the effect on M1 and M3?
cards.back: M1 increases (cash is now in a demand deposit account). M3 is unchanged because M1 is a component of M3 — the funds never left M3.

cards.front: What effect does Fed buying of U.S. government securities in the open market have on the economy?
cards.back: Securities come out of the economy and money goes in. Money supply increases, interest rates fall, borrowing/spending becomes easier, and the economy expands. (Easy money policy)

cards.front: What effect does Fed selling of U.S. government securities in the open market have on the economy?
cards.back: Securities go into the economy and money comes out. Money supply decreases, interest rates rise, borrowing/spending becomes harder, and the economy contracts. (Tight money policy)

cards.front: Which committee directs the Federal Reserve's open-market operations?
cards.back: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). Open-market operations are the most frequently used tool of the FRB.

cards.front: Regulation T
cards.back: An FRB rule setting the minimum amount an investor must deposit when using credit to buy a security. The current initial deposit requirement is 50% of the purchase price (unchanged since 1974).

cards.front: Discount rate
cards.back: The interest rate the Federal Reserve charges member banks for short-term loans (often via repos). It is set by the Fed and viewed as the base rate for the nation.

cards.front: What is the reserve requirement, and what is its current status?
cards.back: Historically, the reserve requirement was the amount a bank had to maintain on deposit with the Fed. As of March 26, 2020, the Fed reduced reserve requirement ratios to 0%, and they remain at 0%. Active policy is now conducted primarily through open-market operations and interest on reserve balances (IORB).

cards.front: Under current Fed practice, what has replaced reserve requirements as a principal policy rate alongside the federal funds target range?
cards.back: Interest on reserve balances (IORB) — formerly known as IOER — which now serves as the floor of the policy rate corridor.

cards.front: Federal funds rate
cards.back: The rate that commercial money center banks charge each other for overnight loans of $1 million or more. Considered a barometer of short-term interest rates and one of the most volatile rates in the economy.

cards.front: Prime rate
cards.back: The interest rate that large U.S. money center commercial banks charge their most creditworthy corporate borrowers for unsecured loans. Set by each bank individually.

cards.front: Broker call loan rate
cards.back: The interest rate banks charge broker-dealers on money borrowed to fund margin account customer loans. Also called the call loan or call money rate; typically about one percentage point above other short-term rates; callable on 24-hour notice.

cards.front: Of the four prominent interest rates (federal funds, prime, broker call, discount), which is set by a federal government body?
cards.back: Only the discount rate is set by the Federal Reserve. The federal funds rate, prime rate, and broker call rate are each set by the financial institutions making the loans.

cards.front: List the actions the Fed takes under an easy money (loose) policy.
cards.back: Buy U.S. government securities in the open market; lower the discount rate; (historically) lower reserve requirements. These actions expand credit and stimulate a slow economy.

cards.front: List the actions the Fed takes under a tight money policy.
cards.back: Sell U.S. government securities in the open market; raise the discount rate; (historically) raise reserve requirements. These actions tighten credit to slow expansion and curb inflation.

cards.front: The FOMC sells Treasury securities in the open market, and the Fed raises the discount rate. What is the likely direction of interest rates?
cards.back: Interest rates will rise. Selling securities pulls money out of the banking system (contracting the money supply), and raising the discount rate makes it more expensive for banks to borrow — both push rates up.

cards.front: What does an increase in the discount rate signal about FRB monetary policy?
cards.back: It signals a tightening of monetary policy. A decreasing discount rate signals an easing of policy.

cards.front: Why does the Fed rarely change reserve requirements (and why did it set them to zero)?
cards.back: Changes to reserve requirements hit all banks simultaneously and have a dramatic, blunt impact across the entire banking system, making them an unwieldy tool. The Fed prefers finer tools like open-market operations and IORB; reserve requirements have been at 0% since March 2020.
